claims.text: Rapid heating and cooling yields noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles with partial phase separation.
Rapid heating and cooling yields elemental segregation in these nanoparticles.
Rapid heating and cooling yields uncontrolled particle morphology in these nanoparticles.
Adding an intermediate thermal hold during cooling effectively slows the cooling regime.
Slower cooling with an intermediate thermal hold increases atomic mobility among the constituent noble metals.
Increased atomic mobility at the hold temperature improves interdiffusion and uniform atomic mixing.
Rapid cooling can kinetically trap the nanoparticles in phase-separated or elementally segregated states because of diffusion limitations.
A thermal hold gives atoms sufficient time to overcome diffusion limitations.
Improved interdiffusion decreases kinetic trapping, phase separation, and elemental segregation.
Improved atomic mixing promotes formation and stabilization of a single-phase solid solution.
Relative to rapid cooling, the modified cooling regime will increase the yield of single-phase nanoparticles.
Relative to rapid cooling, the modified cooling regime will reduce elemental segregation.
The hypothesis applies to noble metal–based high-entropy alloys containing more than five elements and processed under rapid thermal regimes.
The proposed mechanism is limited to compositions for which diffusion kinetics and nucleation behavior dominate phase-purity selection.
The optimal hold temperature and duration depend on the diffusion kinetics of the constituent metals.
